titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Raids south of Valencia; the call to arms; the siege and fall of the city (tiradas 69–74, lines 1156–1220)
part: Tiradas 69–74 · Raids south of Valencia; the call to arms; the siege and fall of the city (lines 1156–1220)

sentences.i: His fame goes ringing abroad; beyond the sea it travels. Glad was the Çid, and all his companies, that God had helped him and given him this victory.
sentences.n: Tirada 69 (assonance á-a) — the Çid's raids south of Valencia (Pidal: Correrías del Cid al sur de Valencia). The line-ends are á-a (compañas, arrancada, trasnochadas, casa, quebranta, entradas; Xátiva counts with them). The tirada takes up the last words of the one before (las nuevas de mio Çid … sonando van, v. 1154): nuevas, 'renown' (Pidal's 'renombre, fama' in his note to v. 1154, which cites v. 1206 for the same sense). alent = allende, 'beyond'; alent parte del mar, 'on the far side of the sea', i.e. over in Africa. [andon] is in italics on the page, a word Pidal supplies; he gives no note, so both the form and the sense are uncertain: it seems to be a form of andar, 'they go, travel' (the tidings). It does not fit the á-a assonance. ayudara, fiziera: the -ra form is here a pluperfect indicative, 'had helped, had made' (fazer = hacer, with the old f-). arrancada, 'rout, victory' (arrancar, 'to rout'). que = 'because'.

sentences.i: He sent out his raiders and they made their marches by night; they reach Cullera and they reach Játiva, and further south still, the town of Denia.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1159: davan means 'enviaban, despachaban', 'sent out, dispatched' (as at v. 1405; compare v. 652). corredores, 'raiders, outriders'; trasnochadas, 'night marches'. Imperfect and present stand side by side (davan, fazien, llegan): epic tense-mixing. Pidal's note to v. 1160: Gujera is the Valencian name Cullera, pronounced with Castilian j; it had an important castle at the mouth of the river Júcar, surrounded by the sea, 30 km from Játiva and 55 from Denia. Xátiva = Játiva (x = [ʃ]). ayusso, 'below, downward' — here 'further south'. Pidal's note to v. 1161: Denia la casa, 'la población de Denia', 'the town of Denia' (compare v. 1232; casa as in Burgos la casa, v. 62).

sentences.t:
cabo del mar tierra de moros firme la quebranta.
Ganaron Peña Cadiella, las exidas e las entradas.
sentences.l:
by the sea land of Moors firmly it he-breaks.
They-won Peña Cadiella, the exits and the entries.
sentences.i: Along the coast he breaks the Moors' land hard. They won Peña Cadiella, its ways out and its ways in.
sentences.n: cabo del mar, 'beside the sea' (cabo = cabe, 'next to'). tierra de moros … la quebranta: the object is put first and picked up again by la, 'the land … he breaks it'. Pidal's note to v. 1163: Peña Cadiella, called Pennacatel in the Latin Historia of the Cid and Peñacadell in various documents, is the modern sierra de Benicadell, which, on the border of the provinces of Valencia and Alicante, divides the valleys of Albaida (north) and Concentaina (south). The Cid rebuilt the castle of Benicadell in 1092; it was a strategic point securing the road from Valencia and Játiva to Alcoy and Alicante. las exidas e las entradas, 'the ways out and the ways in': holding the castle means holding the passes (exir = salir).

sentences.t:
Quando el Çid Campeador ovo Peña Cadiella,
ma’les pesa en Xátiva e dentro en Gujera,
non es con recabdo el dolor de Valençia.
sentences.l:
When the Çid Campeador had Peña Cadiella,
badly-to-them it-weighs in Xátiva and inside in Gujera,
not is with measure the grief of Valençia.
sentences.i: When the Çid Campeador held Peña Cadiella, it weighed sorely on them in Játiva and inside Cullera, and the grief in Valencia was past all bounds.
sentences.n: Tirada 70 (assonance é-a) — the Çid at Peña Cadiella (Pidal: El Cid en Peña Cadiella). Line-ends Cadiella, Gujera, Valençia. ovo, preterite of aver, here 'got, held'. ma'les: Pidal prints the apostrophe and gives no note; the reading is uncertain, most naturally mal les, 'it weighs on them badly', with the l of mal lost before les (pesar a uno, 'to grieve someone'). dentro en, 'inside, within'. con recabdo, 'with measure, under control' (recabdo, 'care, good order'): non es con recabdo, the grief knows no bounds. Pidal gives no note here; the sense is taken from recabdo 'care, strict order' elsewhere (v. 24). Present and preterite again mixed (ovo, pesa, es).

sentences.t:
En tierra de moros prendiendo e ganando,
e durmiendo los días e las noches tranochando,
en ganar aquellas villas mio Çid duró tres años.
sentences.l:
In land of Moors taking and winning,
and sleeping the days and the nights night-marching,
in winning those towns my Çid spent three years.
sentences.i: In the land of the Moors, seizing and winning, sleeping by day and marching through the nights, my Çid spent three years in winning those towns.
sentences.n: Tirada 71 (assonance á-o) — the conquest of the whole region of Valencia (Pidal: Conquista de toda la región de Valencia). Line-ends ganando, tranochando, años. Two lines of gerunds hang in the air until the main verb comes in the third. prender, 'to take, seize' (priso, v. 1095). tranochando = trasnochando, 'marching by night' (trasnochadas, v. 1159), so spelled in Pidal's text. Pidal's note to v. 1169: duró means 'tardó, empleó, gastó', 'took, used up, spent' (compare v. 2251). villas, 'towns'.

sentences.t:
A los de Valençia escarmentados los han,
non osan fueras exir nin con él se ajuntar;
sentences.l:
Those of Valençia chastened them they-have,
not they-dare outside to-go-out nor with him themselves to-join;
sentences.i: They have given the men of Valencia a hard lesson: they dare not come out of the city, nor meet him in the field.
sentences.n: Tirada 72 (assonance á) — the Çid harries Valencia and has war proclaimed to the Christians (Pidal: El Cid asedia a Valencia.—Pregona a los cristianos la guerra). The line-ends are stressed á (han, ajuntar, mal, pan, far …); padre, fanbre and menssajes (á-e) count with them, the final unstressed e being disregarded. A los de Valençia … los han: the object is put first with a (personal a) and taken up again by los; escarmentados los han, 'they have them chastened': aver + participle, the participle agreeing with the object. escarmentar, 'to punish so as to teach a lesson'. fueras = fuera, 'out'; exir = salir. ajuntarse con, 'to join (battle) with'; the pronoun se stands before the infinitive.

sentences.t:
tajávales las huertas e fazíales grand mal,
en cada uno destos años mio Çid les tollió el pan.
sentences.l:
he-was-cutting-to-them the orchards and he-was-doing-to-them great harm,
in each one of-these years my Çid from-them took-away the bread.
sentences.i: He cut down their orchards and did them great harm; in each of those years my Çid took away their bread.
sentences.n: tajávales = tajava les, 'he cut for them' (dative of the person harmed); fazíales likewise. huertas, the irrigated gardens and orchards of the Valencian plain. destos = de estos. tollió, preterite of toller (Latin tollere), 'to take away'. el pan, 'the bread', i.e. the grain harvest.

sentences.t:
Mal se aquexan los de Valençia que non sabent ques far.
de ninguna part que sea non les viníe pan;
sentences.l:
Badly themselves are-pressed those of Valençia that not they-know what-themselves to-do.
from no side that may-be not to-them was-coming bread;
sentences.i: The people of Valencia are sorely pressed, and know not what to do; from no quarter at all did bread come to them.
sentences.n: aquexarse, 'to be hard pressed, distressed'; mal intensifies, 'sorely'. sabent = saben, 3rd plural, the final -t a Latinizing spelling (Latin sapiunt). ques far: Pidal gives no note; it is apparently qué se far, 'what to do' (far = fazer), with se squeezed onto que — the same phrase as at v. 1155, que no saben qué se far; the reading is not certain. The full stop after far is Pidal's, though the sense runs on. de ninguna part que sea, 'from any side whatever'; non … ninguna, the double negative. viníe = venía, imperfect.

sentences.t:
nin da co[n]ssejo padre a fijo, nin fijo a padre,
nin amigo a amigo nos pueden consolar.
sentences.l:
nor gives help father to son, nor son to father,
nor friend to friend not-themselves they-can console.
sentences.i: Father can give son no help, nor son father, nor can friend console friend.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1176: consejo here means 'amparo, socorro', 'shelter, help' — not 'advice'. The n of co[n]ssejo is his (in italics). nin … nin, 'neither … nor'. nos = no se: nos pueden consolar, 'they cannot console one another'. fijo, with Latin f- (modern hijo).

sentences.t:
Mala cueta es, señores, aver mingua de pan,
fijos e mugieres ve[e]r lo[s] murir de fanbre.
sentences.l:
Bad affliction it-is, lords, to-have want of bread,
sons and women to-see them die of hunger.
sentences.i: It is a cruel distress, my lords, to be in want of bread, and to watch children and wives die of hunger.
sentences.n: señores: the minstrel turns to his audience. cueta = cuita, 'affliction, distress'. aver mingua de, 'to be short of' (mingua = mengua). ve[e]r = ver, the old two-syllable veer, its second e Pidal's (in italics); lo[s], the s his too: fijos e mugieres … lo[s], the objects put first and taken up by los. mugieres = mujeres, 'wives, women'. murir = morir; fanbre = hambre (f- for h- again).

sentences.t:
Delante veyen so duelo, non se pueden huviar,
por el rey de Marruecos ovieron a enbiar;
sentences.l:
Before they-were-seeing their grief, not themselves they-can help,
for the king of Marruecos they-had to send;
sentences.i: They saw their ruin before their eyes and could not help themselves; they had to send for the king of Morocco.
sentences.n: Delante, 'before (them)'. veyen = veíen, veían, imperfect of veer, 'they saw' (the y a glide between the vowels; the -ien ending as in fazien, v. 1159), beside the present pueden: tense-mixing again. so = su. huviar, 'to help, succour' (Pidal glosses it 'ayudar' at v. 1183): non se pueden huviar, 'they cannot help themselves'. por … enbiar, 'to send for'. ovieron a enbiar, 'they had to send': aver a + infinitive, 'to have to'. Marruecos, Morocco.

sentences.t:
con el de los Montes Claros, avíe guerra tan grand,
non les dixo co[n]sejo, nin los vino huviar.
sentences.l:
with him of the Montes Claros, he-was-having war so great,
not to-them he-said help, nor them came to-help.
sentences.i: He was waging so great a war with the lord of the Montes Claros that he gave them no help and did not come to their aid.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1182: Montes Claros was the old name for the Atlas range in Morocco. The poet refers anachronistically to the chief of the Almohads, who appear south of the Atlas in 1120 and fight the emperor of Morocco, who died at war with them in 1145. el de los Montes Claros, 'he of the Montes Claros'. avíe = había, 'he had'. Pidal's note to v. 1183: 'he told them no way out of their plight, nor came to help them' (so consejo here, 'a way out, a remedy'; the n of co[n]sejo is Pidal's). vino huviar, venir + bare infinitive, 'came to help' (as viniessen çercar, v. 1099).

sentences.i: My Çid learned of it, and it pleased him to the heart. He rode out of Murviedro one night to march through the dark, and dawn found my Çid in the lands of Monreal.
sentences.n: Sópolo = supo lo, 'he learned it' (saber). de coraçón le plaz, 'it pleases him from the heart'; plaz = place. una noch [a] trasnocha[r]: the a and the final r are Pidal's (in italics), 'one night to march through the night'. amaneció a mio Çid, 'it dawned on my Çid': amanecer used with a + the person, 'day broke for him'. Mon Real: Pidal gives no note here; in his note on Mont Real at vv. 862–864 he identifies it as Monreal del Campo, on the river Jiloca (province of Teruel), and this is presumably the same place, though the poem does not say so.

sentences.t:
Por Aragón e por Navarra pregón mandó echar,
a tierras de Castiella enbió s[o]s menssajes:
sentences.l:
Through Aragón and through Navarra proclamation he-ordered to-cast,
to lands of Castiella he-sent his messages:
sentences.i: Through Aragon and through Navarre he had his proclamation cried, and to the lands of Castile he sent his messages:
sentences.n: pregón mandó echar, 'he ordered a proclamation to be cried' (echar pregón, 'to publish by a crier'; mandar + infinitive, 'to have something done'). s[o]s = sus, the o Pidal's (in italics). menssajes, 'messages' (or the messengers who carry them). Castiella = Castilla, with the old diphthong -iella.

sentences.i: Whoever would be rid of his hardship and come into wealth, let him come to my Çid, who has a mind to ride: he means to besiege Valencia and give it to the Christians.
sentences.n: The proclamation, reported without quotation marks until the next tirada takes it up in direct speech. Pidal's only note to v. 1189 refers to a somewhat similar proclamation on pp. 95–96 of his volume. rritad is the hard word: Pidal gives no gloss on the page, and the sense 'riches, wealth', a noun made on rico, is a likely but uncertain reading (the double rr is the old spelling of initial r). cueta, 'affliction' (v. 1178). viniesse, imperfect subjunctive with the force of a command, 'let him come'. a = ha: a sabor de, 'has a wish to'. a Valençia, personal a before the city, as often. pora cristianos la dar = para darla a cristianos, the pronoun before the infinitive.

sentences.t:
“quien quiere ir comigo çercar a Valençia,
—todos vengan de grado, ninguno non ha premia,—
tres días le speraré en Canal de Çelfa.”
sentences.l:
“who wants to-go with-me to-besiege Valençia,
—all let-them-come of will, none not has compulsion,—
three days him I-will-wait in Canal de Çelfa.”
sentences.i: “Whoever will go with me to besiege Valencia — let all come freely, no one is forced — for three days I will wait for him at the Canal of Celfa.”
sentences.n: Tirada 73 (assonance é-a) — the proclamation repeated (Pidal: Repítese el pregón. (Serie gemela.), 'twin series'): the same matter told again in a new assonance, a favourite device of the poem. Line-ends Valençia, premia, Çelfa. ir … çercar, 'to go to besiege', ir + infinitive without a. de grado, 'willingly'. premia, 'compulsion, constraint'; ninguno non, double negative. le speraré, 'I will wait for him' (him = whoever comes); sperar = esperar. Pidal's note to v. 1194: Celfa lay on the great road that led to Valencia (v. 644); in his note to v. 644 he identifies it as today's Cella, near Teruel.

sentences.t:
Esto dixo mio Çid el [Campeador leal].
Tornávas a Murviedro, ca él ganada se la a.
sentences.l:
This said my Çid the [Campeador loyal].
He-was-returning-himself to Murviedro, for he won for-himself it has.
sentences.i: So spoke my Çid, the loyal Campeador. He went back to Murviedro, for he had won it for himself.
sentences.n: Tirada 74 (assonance á) — men flock to the proclamation; the siege and entry of Valencia (Pidal: Gentes que acuden al pregón.—Cerco y entrada de Valencia). Line-ends leal, a, detardar, cristiandad …; the á-e endings (partes, fazen, caen, alcáç[er]) count with them, as in tirada 72. The whole second half of v. 1195, Campeador leal, is in italics: Pidal's restoration. Campeador, 'the Battler', the Çid's title. Tornávas = tornava se, 'he went back' (se squeezed on). ganada se la a: a = ha; aver + participle agreeing with la (Murviedro), se 'for himself'.

sentences.t:
Andidieron los pregones, sabet, a todas partes,
al sabor de la ganançia, non lo quiere[n] detardar,
grandes yentes se le acojen de la buena cristiandad.
sentences.l:
Went the proclamations, know-ye, to all parts,
at-the relish of the gain, not it they-want to-delay,
great peoples themselves to-him gather of the good Christendom.
sentences.i: The proclamations went out, be sure of it, to every quarter; drawn by the taste of gain, they would not delay: great crowds from good Christendom gather to him.
sentences.n: Andidieron = anduvieron, old strong preterite of andar. sabet, 'know ye' (= sabed): the minstrel's aside to his hearers. al sabor de, 'at the relish of, eager for'. quiere[n], its n Pidal's (in italics). detardar, 'to delay'. yentes = gentes, 'people, men'. se le acojen, 'gather to him' (acojerse a, 'to take refuge with, join').

sentences.t:
Sonando va[n] sus nuevas todas a todas partes;
mas le vienen a mio Çid, sabet, que nos le van;
sentences.l:
Sounding go his tidings all to all parts;
more to-him come to my Çid, know-ye, than not-themselves from-him go;
sentences.i: His fame rings out in every quarter; more men come to my Çid, be sure of it, than leave him.
sentences.n: Lines 1206–1207 are printed here, after v. 1199, though numbered 1206–1207: Pidal moves them up from their place after v. 1205 and keeps their numbers; he gives no reason on the page — presumably because the spreading fame goes with the proclamations going out 'to all parts' (v. 1197). The count then resumes at v. 1200. va[n], its n Pidal's (in italics). nuevas, 'renown' — Pidal's note to v. 1154 cites this line for that sense — and the line echoes the opening of tirada 69 (v. 1156). mas … que, 'more … than'. nos le van = no se le van, 'do not go away from him'; the no seems to be the redundant negative Old Spanish can put after a comparison, so the sense is simply 'than leave him'.

sentences.t:
creçiendo va riqueza a mio Çid el de Bivar;
quando vi[d]o las gentes juntadas, compeçós de pagar.
sentences.l:
growing goes wealth to my Çid he of Bivar;
when he-saw the peoples gathered, began-himself to be-pleased.
sentences.i: Wealth keeps growing for my Çid, he of Vivar; when he saw the men gathered together, he began to be well content.
sentences.n: creçiendo va, ir + gerund: 'goes growing'. vi[d]o = vio, the d Pidal's (in italics), as with vi[d]íe at v. 1096. compeçós = compeçó se, 'he began' (comenzar). pagarse here is 'to be pleased, satisfied', not 'to pay': compeçós de pagar, 'he began to be content'. el de Bivar, 'he of Vivar'.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid don Rodrigo non lo quiso detardar,
adeliñó pora Valençia e sobrellas va echar,
sentences.l:
My Çid don Rodrigo not it wished to-delay,
headed for Valençia and upon-them goes to-cast,
sentences.i: My Çid, Don Rodrigo, would not delay: he made straight for Valencia and goes to throw himself upon them.
sentences.n: don Rodrigo: the Çid's own name, Rodrigo Díaz. detardar, 'to delay' (v. 1198). adeliñar, 'to head straight for'. sobrellas = sobre ellas, 'upon them' (feminine plural: the city and its people, loosely). va echar, ir + bare infinitive (as ferirlos va, v. 1137), echar(se) sobre, 'goes to throw himself upon them', i.e. lays siege.

sentences.t:
bien la çerca mio Çid, que non i avía hart;
viédales exir e viédales entrar.
sentences.l:
well it besieges my Çid, that not there there-was flaw;
he-forbids-to-them to-go-out and he-forbids-to-them to-enter.
sentences.i: My Çid hems it in well, with no flaw in the siege; he lets them neither come out nor go in.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1204: sin art meant 'without deceit', and then 'perfectly' (compare v. 690); so no había en ello art seems to mean 'there was no flaw', the siege was absolutely perfect. hart = art, 'trick, flaw'; Pidal's 'seems' marks the sense as not certain. i = 'there'. çercar, 'to surround, besiege'. viédales = vieda les, 'he forbids them' (vedar, as vedada at v. 62).

sentences.t: Metióla en pla[zd]o, si les viniessen huviar.
sentences.l: He-put-it on term, if to-them they-should-come to-help.
sentences.i: He set the city a term, in case someone should come to their aid.
sentences.n: With v. 1208 the numbered order resumes (1206–1207 having been printed after v. 1199). Pidal's note to v. 1208: 'He set it a term, in case anyone should come to succour them.' According to an Arabic history, the Cid gave the Valencians a last truce of fifteen days to ask for help from the kings of Zaragoza and Murcia, in case they would come to their rescue; when the fifteen days passed without result, Valencia surrendered to the Cid. Metióla = metió la, 'he put it' (la = the city). pla[zd]o = plazo, 'term, set time': the letters zd are in italics, Pidal's restoration, and what stands in the manuscript is not shown on the page. si, 'if, in case'; viniessen huviar, venir + bare infinitive, 'should come to help'.

sentences.t:
Nueve meses complidos, sabet, sobrella yaz,
quando vino el dezeno oviérongela a dar.
sentences.l:
Nine months full, know-ye, upon-it he-lies,
when came the tenth they-had-it-to-him to give.
sentences.i: Nine full months, be sure of it, he lay before the city; when the tenth came, they had to give it up to him.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1209: the siege of Valencia lasted not nine months but twenty; but note that the poet counts these nine months only as a second part of the siege, which begins long before the Cid goes off to raise men, as vv. 1170 ff. tell. complidos = cumplidos, 'full, complete'. sobrella = sobre ella; yaz = yace, 'lies (encamped)', present amid preterites. dezeno, 'tenth' (month). oviérongela a dar: aver a + infinitive, 'they had to give'; gela = ge la, 'it to him' (the ancestor of modern se la).

sentences.t:
Grandes son los gozos que van por [e]s logar
quando mio Çid gañó a Valençia e entró en la çibdad.
sentences.l:
Great are the joys that go through [th]at place
when my Çid won Valençia and entered in the city.
sentences.i: Great is the rejoicing all through that place, when my Çid won Valencia and entered the city.
sentences.n: [e]s logar = ese lugar, its e Pidal's (in italics); the line echoes v. 1146, grand es el gozo que va por es logar. gañó = ganó, 'won'. çibdad = ciudad. Historically Valencia surrendered to the Cid in 1094.

sentences.i: Those who had been foot-soldiers become knights; the gold and the silver — who could count it for you? Every man there was rich.
sentences.n: f[o]ron = fueron, the o Pidal's restored older form (as f[o]sse at v. 61). de pie, 'on foot', foot-soldiers; cavalleros se fazen, 'they become horsemen' — with a horse comes the rank of caballero. vos, 'for you', the audience again; podrie, conditional, 'could'. quantos que allí ha, 'as many as are there' (ha = hay); eran … ha: past and present side by side.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid don Rodrigo la quinta mandó tomar,
en el aver monedado treynta mill marcos le caen,
e los otros averes ¿quien los podrié contar?
sentences.l:
My Çid don Rodrigo the fifth ordered to-take,
in the wealth coined thirty thousand marks to-him fall,
and the other goods who them could count?
sentences.i: My Çid, Don Rodrigo, had his fifth taken: in coined money alone thirty thousand marks fall to his share — and the other riches, who could count them?
sentences.n: la quinta, 'the fifth', the leader's customary share of the booty. aver monedado, 'coined wealth, cash' (aver as a noun, 'goods, property'). marcos, 'marks', a weight of silver (or gold) used as money. le caen, 'fall to him'. averes, 'goods, possessions'. podrié = podría.

sentences.t:
Alegre era el Campeador con todos los que ha,
quando su seña cabdal sedié en somo del alcáç[er].
sentences.l:
Glad was the Campeador with all those that he-has,
when his banner chief was-set on top of-the citadel.
sentences.i: Glad was the Campeador, and all the men he has, when his chief banner stood high upon the citadel.
sentences.n: con todos los que ha, 'with all those he has', his men (ha = has, aver 'to have'). seña cabdal, 'chief standard' (cabdal = caudal, 'principal'). sedié, imperfect of seer, 'to sit, be set'. en somo de, 'on top of'. alcáç[er] = alcázar, 'citadel'; its final er is Pidal's (in italics), which gives the á-e ending that counts with this tirada's á.
